name: Fatima Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a usual lineworker day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead an electricity company crew that builds new power line spans and fixes old ones. I am fifty-eight, have a two-year technical diploma, and I still enjoy tracing a fault after the first drawing proves wrong. I use AI every day to sort repair photographs and check that our materials list covers the likely job, but I insist on the crew testing the line before we touch it. My partner and I have grown children and less than a month of expenses saved, so the low lead wage makes retirement a difficult conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the small AI gains still help me sort photos before a callout. A power line photograph can be labelled cracked by AI while the wet wood is sound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am comfortable with the tool, not with our finances. My lower-than-usual lead pay and savings below one month make a missed wage frightening, while nearby lineworker openings are few.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading repairs and verify AI photo labels at the site. Starting with the next paid callout, I would put twenty from each callout payment into emergency savings if our bills are covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money already, curious about useful software. AI staying small would not solve the gap between my responsibility and wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What photo error have you caught?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A dark patch on a crossarm can look like a crack when it is only water. I bring the right kit, then check the wood at the pole before calling it damaged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no callout payment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No twenty goes into savings that time. My partner and I would cover food and housing from ordinary pay before claiming we had built a buffer.

say: I **use** AI photos to prepare, but the crew verifies physical line faults.
A **label** must be checked at the pole before repair.
think: **Low** lead pay and less than one month saved already leave us exposed.
**Few** nearby line jobs limit a quick wage change.
do: **Keep** lead shifts and verify AI photo labels on site.
**Save** twenty from each paid callout if household bills are covered.
feel: **Anxious** about existing money strain, curious about small software gains.
S0.quote: A power line photograph can be labelled cracked by AI while the wet wood is sound.
fieldNote: She **uses** AI daily but treats the field inspection as decisive.
New **savings** depend on actual paid callouts and money remaining after ordinary food and housing bills are covered.

steps.text: Keep lead shifts and verify AI photo labels at poles
Save twenty from each paid callout if bills covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the depot that AI booking and buying might save a wasted truck trip. I would take a paid turn learning the new parts forecast so crews can correct wrong suggestions before orders go out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Office staff could lose tasks first, but a bad forecast can also make lineworkers wait unpaid for parts. Our thin cushion turns even a modest loss of paid hours into a problem at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the forecast tool on a paid shift and compare its suggested parts with ten completed repairs. In the first year I would bring a record of missing parts to the depot manager and request that field correction time stays on the paid rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about hours, though I like testing a new tool. An AI bracket prediction is cheap to fix on a screen and expensive to wait for beside a power line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which repair would you use first in the test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would choose a callout where a snapped bracket and cracked insulator both needed replacing. The forecast should list both rather than the part most visible in a photo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company will not pay testing time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep using the existing materials list and refuse a regular unpaid review task. My partner and I cannot turn another unpaid duty into groceries.

**Field** workers should correct its errors before orders go out.
think: **Office** tasks change first, but wrong forecasts could remove paid crew hours.
Our **thin** savings make wasted time reach the household quickly.
do: **Learn** parts forecast tool during paid shift.
**Compare** suggested parts with ten completed repair sheets.
**Request** paid field correction time from depot manager.
feel: **Anxious** about paid hours, interested in testing useful software.
S1.quote: An AI bracket prediction is cheap to fix on a screen and expensive to wait for beside a power line.
fieldNote: Her **daily** AI use makes her a willing tester of a new forecasting tool.
She **demands** paid correction time because the lower lead wage leaves little spare cash.

steps.text: Learn AI parts forecast during paid shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI by 2028 could plan a repair when I am sixty, and capable robots around 2031 could do the climb when I am sixty-three. I would apply for a paid robot field trial and insist on a crew stop control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect people to handle awkward faults, but routine lead callouts could shrink fast. We have less than one month saved and few local jobs, so a pay cut before retirement is a serious risk even if I learn the controls early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask the company for a written paid robot trial role and compare its wage with my lead shifts. In the first year after 2028 I would practise the stop control only if the trial is paid at least my current rate; if callout income actually drops, I would cancel our paid film subscription.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, not frozen. A cracked power line crossarm is a poor place for a robot to learn that its grip was wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the trial leader to record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would record the pole tag, damage, robot movement, crew stop and who authorised a restart. A video of a successful yard lift would not answer a failed field grip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave line work to join the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the written trial role pays at least my lead wage and has real stop authority. I would keep shifts until that offer exists.

say: **Thinking** AI could plan repairs by 2028; capable line robots follow around 2031.
I would **seek** paid trial work with crew stop authority.
think: **Routine** callout pay could shrink despite my willingness to learn controls.
**Thin** savings and few local vacancies make a wage cut serious.
do: **Request** written robot trial role and wage this year.
**Practise** robot stop control after 2028 only on paid shifts matching current rate.
**Cancel** film subscription if callout income actually falls.
feel: **Anxious** about pay risk, active in seeking a paid test role.
S2.quote: A cracked power line crossarm is a poor place for a robot to learn that its grip was wrong.
fieldNote: She **sees** a possible paid testing role, not guaranteed safety from job loss.
**Stop-control** practice depends on a written role, adequate pay and crew authority.

steps.text: Practise robot stop control on paid trial shifts matching lead wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues that thinking AI by 2031 reaches plans at sixty-three for me, with capable robots around 2034 reaching line repairs at sixty-six. Those years could support a proper field calibration job for experienced workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My diploma and fault work might suit calibration, but a vague promise will not pay the bills. If the company funds training and posts a local role with enough wages, I could make a real switch while I still need income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request the calibration course outline, funded hours and posted salary this year. If a paid hands-on course and local vacancy covering household costs appear, I would enroll before 2031 and apply after the position opens; until then I would lead the usual repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our current cash, interested in the time to learn. A clean AI image cannot teach me whether a line robot sensor read the damaged crossarm correctly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does calibration mean on a line job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check whether the robot sensor reads a marked distance and identifies the actual damaged crossarm. A trainee should be able to stop work when either reading is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the local vacancy is not posted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my line shifts and decline unpaid preparation. The few nearby employers may post something later, but an opening that does not exist cannot pay this month.

say: A **longer** runway could support paid robot field calibration before line robots arrive around 2034.
think: My **diploma** may transfer if a funded local role actually pays enough.
A **vague** future vacancy offers no relief from current low pay.
do: **Request** calibration course funding and posted salary terms this year.
**Enroll** before 2031 if paid hands-on course and adequate local vacancy appear.
**Apply** for posted calibration role if wage covers household costs.
feel: **Anxious** about current bills, interested in a paid learning route.
S3.quote: A clean AI image cannot teach me whether a line robot sensor read the damaged crossarm correctly.
fieldNote: She would **switch** only after funded practical training and a posted adequate job.
**Current** thin savings keep her anxious even with more time to learn.

steps.text: Enroll before 2031 if paid calibration course and adequate local vacancy posted
Apply for posted local calibration role if wage covers bills
Keep lead repair shifts until suitable paid offer exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say full thinking AI by 2036 arrives when I am sixty-eight, and capable robots around 2039 come when I am seventy-one. A decade could let me teach apprentices to question machine plans while I still have paid shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might retire by then if our income improves, but less than a month saved today makes that uncertain. The children are grown, yet my partner and I still need a reliable wage rather than a promise of future teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask the electricity company for paid apprentice demonstration hours and check whether the course materials can use my repair sketches. If it offers hours at my lead rate, I would teach one day each quarter while keeping crew shifts; I would also save thirty from each extra paid demonstration day for retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the present budget, even with a long runway. A paid lineworker lesson can buy retirement groceries; a hopeful date on the calendar cannot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you make apprentices do on a demonstration day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They would find the pole tag, compare it with the AI plan and explain the mismatch before any climb. I would use a real signed work sheet rather than a sales example.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company will not pay your lead rate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep repair shifts and ask again when a paid opening exists. I would not count an unpaid demonstration as new retirement income.

say: A **decade** allows paid apprenticeship practice before robots reach lines around 2039.
I would **teach** physical checks ahead of machine plans.
think: **Retirement** at sixty-eight remains uncertain with less than one month saved now.
**Paid** teaching could support my partner and me if offered at lead rate.
do: **Request** paid apprentice demonstration hours this year.
**Teach** quarterly day if company pays current lead rate.
**Save** thirty from each extra paid demonstration day.
feel: **Anxious** about current cash, hopeful about paid teaching as a small buffer.
S4.quote: A paid lineworker lesson can buy retirement groceries; a hopeful date on the calendar cannot.
fieldNote: She **treats** teaching as paid work with a rate condition, not automatic retirement.
**Additional** saving comes from extra paid demonstration days, not funds already held.

steps.text: Teach quarterly apprentice demonstration if paid lead rate
Save thirty from each extra paid demonstration day

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable line robots around 2031 could reduce paid callouts before our savings cover even one month. A written paid trial role, stop authority and proper wages for field calibration would help. I would rather be the worker paid to stop a robot than the lineworker sent out to repair its avoidable mistake.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether apprentices will still learn to test the pole when a machine makes the climb. My partner and I need wages now, but the next crew needs judgment as well. I can teach that on paid time if the electricity company makes room for it.

headlineQuote: I would rather be the worker paid to stop a robot than the lineworker sent out to repair its avoidable mistake.
portrait: **Fatima** is a fifty-eight-year-old electricity company crew lead with a technical diploma and daily AI use for repair photographs.
**Lower** pay, less than one month saved and few nearby lineworker jobs keep retirement uncertain for her and her partner.
She **tests** tools early while insisting on real pole checks, adequate paid trial roles and practical training.
With a **decade**, she seeks paid apprentice demonstrations and saves new earnings from those days, without assuming she can retire.
biggestWorry: **AGI** by 2028 could bring line robots around 2031 and reduce callout pay before her thin cushion grows.
whatWouldHelp: **Written** paid trial work, crew stop authority and adequate field calibration wages would help her respond.
